claim: Both top-down and bottom-up signals underlie perception.
source: There is a growing understanding that both top-down and bottom-up signals underlie perception.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established understanding in the field.

claim: Predictive coding theories describe integration of top-down and bottom-up signals in terms of how well top-down predictions fit with bottom-up sensory input.
source: 'Predictive coding' theories describe this integration in terms of how well top-down predictions fit with bottom-up sensory input.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory presented in the abstract.

claim: The study combined EEG methods that preferentially tag different levels in the visual hierarchy.
source: To achieve this, we combined EEG methods that preferentially tag different levels in the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Intermodulation components were examined as a measure of integration between top-down and bottom-up signals.
source: Importantly, we examined intermodulation components as a measure of integration between these signals.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Top-down predictions integrate with bottom-up signals in a manner modulated by the predictability of sensory input.
source: Our results link the different signals to core aspects of predictive coding, and suggest that top-down predictions indeed integrate with bottom-up signals in a manner that is modulated by the predictability of the sensory input, providing evidence for predictive coding and opening new avenues to studying such interactions in perception.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Prior experience, expectations and knowledge allow for the formation of priors or hypotheses about the state of the external world.
source: Prior experience, expectations and knowledge about the world allow for the formation of priors or hypotheses about the state of the external world (i.e., the causes of the sensory input) that help, via top-down signals, resolve ambiguity in bottom-up sensory signals.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about predictive coding presented in the introduction.

claim: Early models of neural processing implementing predictive coding explicitly incorporated prior knowledge of statistical regularities in the environment.
source: Early models of neural processing implementing such a predictive coding framework explicitly incorporated prior knowledge of statistical regularities in the environment (Srinivasan et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Srinivasan et al., 1982.

claim: Contemporary accounts treat predictive coding ideas in terms of Bayesian inference and prediction error minimization.
source: Contemporary accounts treat these ideas in terms of Bayesian inference and prediction error minimization (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005; Friston and Stephan, 2007; Hohwy, 2013; Clark, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Perception is essentially an inferential process.
source: That perception is essentially an inferential process is supported by many behavioural findings demonstrating the significant role of contextual information (Geisler and Kersten, 2002; Kersten et al., 2004; Kok and Lange, 2015; Weiss et al., 2002) and of top-down signals (Kok et al., 2012b, Pascual-Leone and Walsh, 2001; Ro et al., 2003; Vetter et al., 2014) in perception.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Different neural measures exist for feedforward and feedback signals primarily in terms of their characteristic oscillatory frequency bands.
source: Several studies additionally suggest different neural measures of feedforward and feedback signals (Hupe et al., 1998) primarily in terms of their characteristic oscillatory frequency bands (Bastos et al., 2015; Buschman and Miller, 2007; Fontolan et al., 2014; Mayer et al., 2016; Michalareas et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2016; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: SWIFT constantly activates low-level visual areas while periodically engaging high-level visual areas.
source: To preferentially track top-down signals (i.e., putative prediction signals) we used semantic wavelet induced frequency tagging (SWIFT) that has been shown to constantly activate low-level visual areas while periodically engaging high-level visual areas (thus, selectively tagging the high-level visual areas; [Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013; Koenig-Robert et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous SWIFT studies.

claim: The study combined SWIFT and SSVEP methods by presenting SWIFT-modulated images at 1.3 Hz while modulating global luminance at 10 Hz.
source: We combined the two methods by presenting SWIFT-modulated images at 1.3 HZ while modulating the global luminance of the stimulus at 10 Hz to elicit SSVEP (See Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Intermodulation components appear as a marker of integration between differentially tagged signals.
source: Critically, we hypothesized that intermodulation (IM) components would appear as a marker of integration between these differentially tagged signals.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: When input signal is comprised of more than one fundamental frequency that interact within a non-linear system, the response output will show additional frequencies as linear combinations of the input frequencies.
source: When the input signal is comprised of more than one fundamental frequency (e.g., F1 and F2) that interact within a non-linear system, the response output will show additional frequencies as linear combinations of the input frequencies (e.g., f1 +f2, f1 - f2, etc.)
evidence: This is a description of the intermodulation phenomenon based on established knowledge.

claim: Intermodulation components in EEG recordings have been used to study non-linear interactions in the visual system.
source: Intermodulation components in EEG recordings have been used to study non-linear interactions in the visual system (Clynes, 1961; Regan and Regan, 1988; Zemon and Ratliff, 1984), with some recent applications for the study of high-level visual-object recognition systems (Boremanse et al., 2013; Gundlach and Müller, 2013; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using intermodulation.

claim: Expectation reflects the continuous process of probabilistic learning about what is possible or probable in the forthcoming sensory environment.
source: One such property is expectation, which reflects the continuous process of probabilistic learning about what is possible or probable in the forthcoming sensory environment (Summerfield and Egner, 2009) and therefore plays a central role in predictive coding.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Summerfield and Egner, 2009.

claim: Various studies have demonstrated the relationship between stimulus predictability and neural responses.
source: Indeed, various studies have demonstrated the relationship between stimulus predictability and neural responses (Kok et al., 2012a, Todorovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Certainty was manipulated by changing the frequency of images in each trial.
source: Certainty was manipulated by changing the frequency of images in each trial; the more frequent the image is presented, the easier to successfully predict what the next stimulus will be.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: Belief updates occur by combining predictions derived from prior probabilities with sensory-driven data, resulting in prediction errors which are weighted by their relative precisions.
source: From the viewpoint of Bayesian belief updating, belief updates occur by combining predictions derived from prior probabilities with sensory-driven data, resulting in prediction errors which are weighted by their relative precisions (Mathys et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mathys et al., 2014.

claim: The certainty manipulation affected the precision of predictions such that higher certainty means higher prior precision and less weighting for the bottom-up prediction error.
source: The certainty manipulation thus affected the precision of predictions such that higher certainty means higher prior precision and less weighting for the bottom-up prediction error.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental manipulation in terms of predictive coding theory.

claim: The precision of the stimuli themselves did not vary across trials.
source: The precision of the stimuli themselves (e.g. the level of noise in the stimulus) did not vary across trials.
evidence: This describes a control aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Participants were presented with 50 s 'movie' streams in which either a house or a face image appeared briefly at a frequency of 1.3 Hz.
source: Participants were presented with 50 s 'movie' streams in which either a house or a face image appeared briefly at a frequency of 1.3 Hz (F2).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each 50 s trial was constructed using one face and one house image randomly selected from a pool of images.
source: Each 50 s trial was constructed using one face and one house image randomly selected from a pool of images.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Images were scrambled using two frequency tagging methods - SWIFT and SSVEP - that differentially tag areas in the cortical hierarchy.
source: Images were scrambled using two frequency tagging methods - SWIFT and SSVEP - that differentially tag areas in the cortical hierarchy (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and references Figure 1.

claim: Participants were instructed to count the number of times one of the two images appeared in the trial.
source: Prior to each trial, participants were instructed to count the number of times one of the two images appeared in the trial (either the house or the face image) and they reported their response at the end of each trial.
evidence: This describes the task given to participants.

claim: The proportion of images changed over trials, ranging from trials in which both images appeared in nearly half the cycles to trials in which one of the images appeared in nearly all cycles.
source: The proportion of images changed over trials, ranging from trials in which both images appeared in nearly half the cycles (referred to as 'low certainty' trials) to trials in which one of the images appeared in nearly all cycles (referred to as 'high certainty' trials).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of certainty.

claim: A pool of 28 face and 28 house images were used in the paradigm.
source: A pool of 28 face and 28 house images were used in the paradigm (images with 'free to use, share or modify, even commercially' usage rights, obtained from Google Images).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cyclic local-contour scrambling in the wavelet-domain allows modulation of the semantics of the image at a given frequency while keeping low-level principal physical attributes constant over time.
source: Cyclic local-contour scrambling in the wavelet-domain allows us to modulate the semantics of the image at a given frequency (i.e. the tagging-frequency, F2 = 1.3 hz, illustrated by the red line) while keeping low-level principal physical attributes constant over time (illustrated by the blue line)
evidence: This describes the SWIFT principle and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Significant peaks were observed at both tagging frequencies (f1 = 10 Hz and f2 = 1.3 Hz) and their harmonics.
source: Importantly, significant peaks can be seen at both tagging frequencies (f1 = 10 Hz and f2 = 1.3 Hz) and their harmonics (n1f1 and n2f2 where n1 = 1,2 and n2 = 1,2,3...8 and 11; red and pink solid lines in Figure 2) and at various IM components (n1f1 + n2f2 where n1 = 1, n2 = +−1,+−2,+−3,+−4 as well as n1 = 2, n2 = −1,+2; orange dashed lines in Figure 2) (one sample t-test, FDR-adjusted p<0.01 for frequencies of interest in the range of 1 Hz–40Hz).
evidence: This is a finding from the FFT analysis shown in Figure 2, supported by statistical testing.

claim: Significant peaks were observed at various IM components.
source: Importantly, significant peaks can be seen at both tagging frequencies (f1 = 10 Hz and f2 = 1.3 Hz) and their harmonics (n1f1 and n2f2 where n1 = 1,2 and n2 = 1,2,3...8 and 11; red and pink solid lines in Figure 2) and at various IM components (n1f1 + n2f2 where n1 = 1, n2 = +−1,+−2,+−3,+−4 as well as n1 = 2, n2 = −1,+2; orange dashed lines in Figure 2) (one sample t-test, FDR-adjusted p<0.01 for frequencies of interest in the range of 1 Hz–40Hz).
evidence: This is a finding from the FFT analysis shown in Figure 2, supported by statistical testing.

claim: SSVEP amplitude SNRs were strongest over the occipital region.
source: SSVEP amplitude signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) were strongest, as expected, over the occipital region (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the topography analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Highest SWIFT SNRs were found over more temporo- and centro-parietal electrodes.
source: For SWIFT, highest SNRs were found over more temporo- and centro-parietal electrodes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the topography analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Strongest SNR values for the IM components were found over occipital electrodes.
source: Strongest SNR values for the IM components were indeed found over occipital electrodes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the topography analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The distributions of all IM components were significantly more correlated with the SSVEP than with the SWIFT distribution.
source: We found that the distributions of all IM components were significantly more correlated with the SSVEP than with the SWIFT distribution (z = 6.44, z = 5.52, z = 6.5 and z = 6.03 for f1+f2, f1−f2, f1+2f2 and f1−2f2, respectively; two-tailed, FDR adjusted p<0.01 for all comparisons; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, supported by statistical testing.

claim: The primary visual cortex is known to be a principal source of SSVEP.
source: We expected to find strongest SSVEP amplitudes over the occipital region (as the primary visual cortex is known to be a principal source of SSVEP [Di Russo et al., 2007])
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Di Russo et al., 2007.

claim: SWIFT has been shown to increasingly activate higher areas in the visual pathway.
source: and strongest SWIFT amplitudes over more temporal and parietal regions (as SWIFT has been shown to increasingly activate higher areas in the visual pathway [Koenig-Robert et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koenig-Robert et al., 2015.

claim: Under the predictive coding framework, predictions are projected to lower levels in the cortical hierarchy where they are integrated with sensory input.
source: Under the predictive coding framework, predictions are projected to lower levels in the cortical hierarchy where they are integrated with sensory input.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: IM signals will be found primarily over occipital regions.
source: We therefore speculated that IM signals will be found primarily over occipital regions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Certainty had a different effect on the SSVEP, SWIFT and IM signals.
source: Using likelihood ratio tests with linear mixed models (see Materials and methods) we found that certainty indeed had a different effect on the SSVEP, SWIFT and IM signals (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: SSVEP was not significantly modulated by certainty.
source: First, SSVEP (log of SNR at f1 = 10 Hz) was not significantly modulated by certainty (all Chi square and p-values are shown in Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: SSVEP reflects mainly low-level visual processing which should be mostly unaffected by the degree of certainty about the incoming signals.
source: This result is consistent with the interpretation of SSVEP as mainly reflecting low-level visual processing which should be mostly unaffected by the degree of certainty about the incoming signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SSVEP finding based on predictive coding theory.

claim: SWIFT signals significantly decreased in trials with higher certainty.
source: Second, the SWIFT signals (log of SNR at f2 = 1.3 Hz) significantly decreased in trials with higher certainty.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: SWIFT is related to the origin of top-down signals which are modulated by certainty.
source: This is consistent with an interpretation of SWIFT as being related to the origin of top-down signals which are modulated by certainty.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SWIFT finding based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Better, more certain predictions would elicit less weighting for the prediction error and therefore less revisions of the high level semantic representation.
source: Specifically, better, more certain predictions would elicit less weighting for the prediction error and therefore less revisions of the high level semantic representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SWIFT finding based on predictive coding theory.

claim: IM signals were found to increase as a function of increasing certainty for three of the four IM components.
source: Critically, the IM signals were found to increase as a function of increasing certainty for three of the four IM components (f1−2f2 = 7.4 Hz, f1−f2 = 8.7 Hz, and f1+2f2 = 12.6 Hz though not for f1+f2 = 11.3 Hz; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The effect of certainty on IM remained highly significant when including all four IM components in one model.
source: The effect remained highly significant also when including all four IM components in one model.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: IMs reflect the efficacy of integration between top-down, prediction-driven signals and bottom-up sensory input.
source: Indeed, this is the effect we would expect to find if IMs reflect the efficacy of integration between top-down, prediction-driven signals and bottom-up sensory input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IM finding based on predictive coding theory.

claim: In high-certainty trials the same image appeared in the majority of cycles, allowing for the best overall correspondence between predictions and bottom-up sensory signals.
source: In high-certainty trials the same image appeared in the majority of cycles, allowing for the best overall correspondence between predictions and bottom-up sensory signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The certainty slope was significantly higher for the IM than for SSVEP.
source: The certainty slope was significantly higher for the IM than for SSVEP (χ2 = 12.49, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis comparing slopes.

claim: The certainty slope was significantly lower for SWIFT than for SSVEP.
source: and significantly lower for SWIFT than for SSVEP (χ2 = 64.45, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis comparing slopes.

claim: Key to perception is the ability to integrate neural information derived from different levels of the cortical hierarchy.
source: Key to perception is the ability to integrate neural information derived from different levels of the cortical hierarchy (Fahrenfort et al., 2012; Tononi and Edelman, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fahrenfort et al., 2012 and Tononi and Edelman, 1998.

claim: SSVEP and SWIFT methods have been shown to predominantly tag low levels (V1/V2) and higher, semantically rich levels in the visual hierarchy, respectively.
source: Hierarchical Frequency Tagging combines the SSVEP and SWIFT methods that have been shown to predominantly tag low levels (V1/V2) and higher, semantically rich levels in the visual hierarchy, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the methods based on previous research.

claim: SSVEP and SWIFT signals reflect bottom-up sensory-driven signals (or prediction errors) and top-down predictions.
source: We hypothesised that these signals reflect bottom-up sensory-driven signals (or prediction errors) and top-down predictions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: Intermodulation components reflect the level of integration between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory-driven input.
source: Critically, we considered intermodulation (IM) components as an indicator of integration between these signals and hypothesised that they reflect the level of integration between top-down predictions (of different strengths manipulated by certainty) and bottom-up sensory-driven input.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: The scalp topography for SSVEP, SWIFT and IMs were largely consistent with the study's hypotheses.
source: Indeed, the scalp topography for the three frequency categories (SSVEP, SWIFT and IMs) were, as we discuss further below, largely consistent with our hypotheses (Figure 3)
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: SSVEP signals were not significantly modulated by certainty.
source: While SSVEP signals were not significantly modulated by certainty, the SWIFT signals decreased and the IM signals increased as a function of increasing certainty (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: SWIFT signals decreased as a function of increasing certainty.
source: While SSVEP signals were not significantly modulated by certainty, the SWIFT signals decreased and the IM signals increased as a function of increasing certainty (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: IM signals increased as a function of increasing certainty.
source: While SSVEP signals were not significantly modulated by certainty, the SWIFT signals decreased and the IM signals increased as a function of increasing certainty (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ibn al Haytham noted in the 11th century that many visible properties are perceived by judgment and inference in addition to sensing the object's form.
source: The notion of perceptual inference and the focus on prior expectations goes back as far as Ibn al Haytham in the 11th century who noted that 'Many visible properties are perceived by judgment and inference in addition to sensing the object's form' (Sabra, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sabra, 1989.

claim: Hypotheses about the state of the external world are formed on the basis of prior experience.
source: Under the predictive coding framework, hypotheses about the state of the external world are formed on the basis of prior experience.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: Predictions are generated from hypotheses, which are then projected to lower levels in the cortical hierarchy, and continually tested and adjusted in light of the incoming, stimulus-driven, information.
source: Predictions are generated from these hypotheses, which are then projected to lower levels in the cortical hierarchy, and continually tested and adjusted in light of the incoming, stimulus-driven, information.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: The role of top-down signals in perception has been demonstrated in both animal and human studies.
source: Indeed, the role of top-down signals in perception has been demonstrated in both animal and human studies (Hupe et al., 1998, Pascual-Leone and Walsh, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hupe et al., 1998 and Pascual-Leone and Walsh, 2001.

claim: The elements of the sensory input that cannot be explained away by the current top-down predictions are referred to as the prediction error.
source: The elements of the sensory input that cannot be explained away by the current top-down predictions are referred to as the prediction error (PE).
evidence: This is a definition from predictive coding theory.

claim: The prediction error is suggested to be the (precision weighted) bottom-up signal that propagates from lower to higher levels in the cortical hierarchy until it can be explained away.
source: This PE is suggested to be the (precision weighted) bottom-up signal that propagates from lower to higher levels in the cortical hierarchy until it can be explained away, allowing for subsequent revisions of higher-level parts of the overall hypotheses.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: The notion of prediction errors has been validated by numerous studies.
source: The notion of PEs has been validated by numerous studies (Hughes et al., 2001; Kellermann et al., 2016; Lee and Nguyen, 2001; Todorovic et al., 2011; Wacongne et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several studies suggest that top-down and bottom-up signals can be differentiated in terms of their typical oscillatory frequency bands.
source: and several studies suggest that top-down and bottom-up signals can be differentiated in terms of their typical oscillatory frequency bands (Fontolan et al., 2014; Sedley et al., 2016; Sherman et al., 2016; Michalareas et al., 2016; Mayer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Perception is achieved by an iterative process that singles out the hypothesis that best minimizes the overall prediction error across multiple levels of the cortical hierarchy while taking prior learning, the wider context, and precision estimations into account.
source: Perception, under the predictive coding framework, is achieved by an iterative process that singles out the hypothesis that best minimizes the overall prediction error across multiple levels of the cortical hierarchy while taking prior learning, the wider context, and precision estimations into account (Friston, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Friston, 2009.

claim: Constant integration of bottom-up and top-down neural information is understood to be a crucial element in perception.
source: Constant integration of bottom-up and top-down neural information is therefore understood to be a crucial element in perception (Fahrenfort et al., 2012; Friston, 2005; Tononi and Edelman, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The SSVEP method predominantly tags activity in low levels of the visual hierarchy.
source: The SSVEP method predominantly tags activity in low levels of the visual hierarchy and indeed highest SSVEP SNRs were measured in our design over occipital electrodes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the topography analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The SSVEP signal reflects persistent bottom-up sensory input, which does not strongly depend on top-down predictions occurring at the SWIFT frequency.
source: These findings suggest that the SSVEP reflects persistent bottom-up sensory input, which does not strongly depend on top-down predictions occurring at the SWIFT frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SSVEP findings.

claim: The SWIFT method has been shown to increasingly tag higher areas along the visual pathway which process semantic information.
source: The SWIFT method, in contrast, has been shown to increasingly tag higher areas along the visual pathway which process semantic information (Koenig-Robert et al., 2015), and we indeed found highest SWIFT SNRs over more temporal and parietal electrodes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koenig-Robert et al., 2015 and findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: The activation of higher visual areas depends on image recognition.
source: Since the activation of these areas depends on image recognition (Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013), we hypothesised that contrary to the SSVEP, the SWIFT signal should show greater dependency on certainty.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013.

claim: SWIFT SNR decreased as certainty levels increased.
source: Indeed, we observed that SWIFT SNR decreased as certainty levels increased (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The SWIFT SNR decline with certainty reflects the decreasing weight on PE signals under high certainty.
source: One interpretation of this result is that it reflects the decreasing weight on PE signals under high certainty (which in turn drive the subsequent top-down predictions).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SWIFT finding based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Various studies have previously demonstrated that highly predictable stimuli tend to evoke reduced neural responses.
source: Indeed, various studies have previously demonstrated that highly predictable stimuli tend to evoke reduced neural responses (Alink et al., 2010; Todorovic and de Lange, 2012; Todorovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Reduced neural responses to predictable stimuli have been suggested to reflect decreased PE signals.
source: Since PEs reflect the elements of sensory input that cannot be explained by predictions, such reduced neural responses have been suggested to reflect decreased PE signals (Todorovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Todorovic et al., 2011.

claim: The SWIFT SNR decline with certainty can be described in terms of neural adaptation (or repetition suppression).
source: The SWIFT SNR decline with certainty can also be described in terms of neural adaptation (or repetition suppression), that is, the reduction in the evoked neural response measured upon repetition of the same stimulus or when the stimulus is highly expected.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the SWIFT finding.

claim: High-certainty trials contained more consecutive cycles in which the same image was presented, thus adaptation is expected to occur.
source: In our current study, high-certainty trials contained more consecutive cycles in which the same image was presented, thus adaptation is expected to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: From the predictive coding perspective, adaptation is explained in terms of increasing precision of predictions stemming from perceptual learning.
source: From the predictive coding perspective, however, adaptation is explained in terms of increasing precision of predictions stemming from perceptual learning (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016; Friston, 2005; Henson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016; Friston, 2005; and Henson, 2003.

claim: Adaptation reflects a reduction in perceptual 'prediction error' that occurs when sensory evidence conforms to a more probable (previously seen), compared to a less probable (novel), percept.
source: Adaptation then 'reflects a reduction in perceptual 'prediction error'… that occurs when sensory evidence conforms to a more probable (previously seen), compared to a less probable (novel), percept.' (Summerfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Summerfield et al., 2008.

claim: The strength of the Hierarchical Frequency Tagging (HFT) paradigm is in its potential ability to obtain, through the occurrence of IM, a direct electrophysiological measure of integration between signals derived from different levels in the cortical hierarchy.
source: Accordingly, the strength of the Hierarchical Frequency Tagging (HFT) paradigm is in its potential ability to obtain, through the occurrence of IM, a direct electrophysiological measure of integration between signals derived from different levels in the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The presence of IM components simply imply a non-linear integration of the steady-state responses elicited by the SWIFT and SSVEP manipulations.
source: From the most general perspective, the presence of IM components simply imply a non-linear integration of the steady-state responses elicited by the SWIFT and SSVEP manipulations.
evidence: This is a general interpretation of the IM findings.

claim: Various biologically plausible neural circuits for implementing nonlinear neuronal operations have been suggested.
source: Various biologically plausible neural circuits for implementing nonlinear neuronal operations have been suggested (Kouh and Poggio, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kouh and Poggio, 2008.

claim: The presence of IMs in themselves cannot point conclusively at specific computational or neuronal processes to which the IMs could be mapped.
source: The presence of IMs in themselves therefore cannot point conclusively at specific computational or neuronal processes to which the IMs could be mapped.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the IM interpretation.

claim: Suggesting IMs as evidence for predictive coding rather than other theories of perception remains to some degree indirect.
source: Suggesting IMs as evidence for predictive coding rather than other theories of perception therefore remains to some degree indirect, however, various arguments indeed point to the recurrent and top-down mediation of the IM responses in our data.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the interpretation.

claim: The scalp distributions of the IM components were more strongly correlated to the spatial distribution of the SSVEP rather than to the SWIFT.
source: First, the scalp distributions of the IM components were more strongly correlated to the spatial distribution of the SSVEP (f1 = 10 Hz) rather than to the SWIFT (f2 = 1.3 Hz) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IM components in HFT data reflect the integration of signals generated in SWIFT-tagged areas which project to, and are integrated with, signals generated at lower levels of the visual cortex, as tagged by the SSVEP.
source: This pattern supports the notion that the IM components in our Hierarchical Frequency Tagging (HFT) data reflect the integration of signals generated in SWIFT-tagged areas which project to, and are integrated with, signals generated at lower levels of the visual cortex, as tagged by the SSVEP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the topography findings.

claim: This is consistent with the predictive coding framework in which predictions generated at higher levels in the cortical hierarchy propagate to lower areas in the hierarchy where they can be tested in light of incoming sensory-driven signals.
source: This of course is consistent with the predictive coding framework in which predictions generated at higher levels in the cortical hierarchy propagate to lower areas in the hierarchy where they can be tested in light of incoming sensory-driven signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the findings to predictive coding theory.

claim: The IM SNRs increased as a function of certainty (contrary to the SWIFT SNR).
source: Second, and more importantly, the IM SNRs increased as a function of certainty (contrary to the SWIFT SNR).
evidence: This is a summary of the IM findings.

claim: This result lends specific support to the predictive coding framework where translating predictions into prediction errors rests upon nonlinear functions.
source: We suggest that this result lends specific support to the predictive coding framework where translating predictions into prediction errors rests upon nonlinear functions (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016.

claim: Nonlinearities in predictive coding models are a specific corollary of top-down modulatory signals.
source: Indeed, nonlinearities in predictive coding models are a specific corollary of top-down modulatory signals (Friston, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Friston, 2005.

claim: Varying certainty levels would be expected to impact IM signal strength through the nonlinear modulation of bottom-up input by top-down predictions.
source: Varying certainty levels, as operationalised in our stimuli, would therefore be expected to impact IM signal strength through the nonlinear modulation of bottom-up input by top-down predictions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IM findings based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Higher certainty trials induced greater predictability of upcoming images and a greater overall match throughout the trial between predictions and sensory input.
source: Specifically, higher certainty trials induced greater predictability of upcoming images and a greater overall match throughout the trial between predictions and sensory input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The increase in IM SNRs may reflect the efficient integration of, or the overall 'fit' between, predictions and sensory input that should be expected when much of the upcoming stimuli is highly predictable.
source: The increase in IM SNRs in our data may therefore reflect the efficient integration of, or the overall 'fit' between, predictions and sensory input that should be expected when much of the upcoming stimuli is highly predictable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IM findings.

claim: Top-down nonlinearities are driven by the conditional expectations of the hidden causes and the conditional expectations of the hidden states.
source: According to the model set forward by Auksztulewicz and Friston (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016), for example, top-down nonlinearities (functions g and f in equations 6 and 7, as well as in Figure 1 in that work) are driven by two elements: (1) the conditional expectations of the hidden causes (µv, i.e. the brain's 'best estimate' as to what is driving the changes in the physical world), and (2) the conditional expectations of the hidden states (µx, i.e. the brain's best estimate about the actual 'physics' of the external world that drives the responses of the sensory organs).
evidence: This is a description of a model from Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016.

claim: The conditional expectations of hidden causes and states may be suggested to be driven primarily by the SWIFT and the SSVEP, respectively.
source: Appealing to this model, the conditional expectations of hidden causes and states may be suggested to be driven primarily by the SWIFT (tagging activity in areas rich in semantic information) and the SSVEP (tagging activity in areas responding to low-level visual features), respectively.
evidence: This is a proposed mapping of the study's findings to a theoretical model.

claim: Top-down predictions can be expected to result in the formation of the IM components that reflect the nonlinear integration of SWIFT- and SSVEP-driven signals.
source: Top-down predictions can therefore be expected to result in the formation of the IM components that reflect the nonlinear integration of SWIFT- and SSVEP-driven signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the findings relate to predictive coding theory.

claim: One interpretation is that the IMs collectively encode (some approximation to the log) model evidence.
source: One such interpretation is that the IMs collectively encode (some approximation to the log) model evidence.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the IM findings.

claim: This notion is compatible with the interpretation of IMs in terms of the 'fit' between predictions and sensory input.
source: This notion is compatible with our interpretation of IMs in terms of the 'fit' between predictions and sensory input.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of interpretations.

claim: One would expect the IMs to increase with certainty if IMs encode model evidence.
source: In this case, one would expect the IMs to increase with certainty, as shown in Figure 5c.
evidence: This is an inference based on the interpretation and findings shown in Figure 5c.

claim: IM findings may arise from sensory processing alone through interactions between neurons modulated by stimulus contrast via SSVEP and neurons modulated by category information via SWIFT.
source: One could potentially argue that our IM findings may arise from sensory processing alone. For example, consider a population of neurons confined within the visual cortex, in which some are modulated by stimulus contrast via SSVEP and some are modulated by category information via SWIFT. Interactions between these neurons, in such an essentially feedforward mechanism, may potentially account for the formation of IM components even without any top-down signals.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claim: The alternative feedforward interpretation cannot easily account for the pattern of reciprocal changes with certainty found in the data (decreasing SWIFT and increasing IMs).
source: However, this alternative interpretation cannot easily account for the pattern of reciprocal changes with certainty found in our data (decreasing SWIFT and increasing IMs).
evidence: This is a counterargument to the alternative interpretation.

claim: Integration of bottom-up sensory input alone should be blind to the probabilistic properties of the trial.
source: Integration of bottom-up sensory input alone should be blind to the probabilistic properties of the trial such that accounting for the pattern of data here requires suggesting an additional local mechanism which is sensitive to the certainty manipulation.
evidence: This is a logical argument against the alternative interpretation.

claim: It seems more reasonable to assume an interaction between early and higher sensory areas, which have been shown to be sensitive to the predictability of stimuli.
source: Therefore, it seems more reasonable to assume an interaction between early and higher sensory areas, which have been shown to be sensitive to the predictability of stimuli (Kok et al., 2012a, Rauss et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kok et al., 2012a and Rauss et al., 2011.

claim: The IM components could in principle result from the integration of low-level SSVEP signals with minimal, non-semantic, SWIFT-driven signals entrained in the early visual cortex.
source: In addition, the IM components could in principle result from the integration of low-level SSVEP signals with minimal, non-semantic, SWIFT-driven signals entrained in the early visual cortex (e.g. by residual tagging of the noise components within the SWIFT frames).
evidence: This is another alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claim: Previous findings suggest that SWIFT does not tag V1-level activity as no tagging could be detected neither for trials in which non-semantic patterns were used nor for trials in which attention was driven away from the image.
source: While this possibility cannot be fully excluded, previous findings suggest that SWIFT does not tag V1-level activity as no tagging could be detected neither for trials in which non-semantic patterns were used nor for trials in which attention was driven away from the image (Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013; Koenig-Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013 and Koenig-Robert et al., 2015.

claim: Residual low-level SWIFT-tagging is not likely to be the primary contributor to the IM components found here.
source: Residual low-level SWIFT-tagging is therefore not likely to be the primary contributor to the IM components found here.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on previous findings.

claim: Several studies have demonstrated a relationship between IM components and perception.
source: Several studies have demonstrated a relationship between IM components and perception (Boremanse et al., 2013; Gundlach and Müller, 2013; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In previous studies, the reported increase in IM signal strength potentially reflects the integration of different input elements within a single neural representation.
source: In all of these studies, the reported increase in IM signal strength potentially reflects the integration of different input elements within a single neural representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous studies.

claim: The strength of Hierarchical Frequency Tagging is in its ability to simultaneously tag both bottom-up and top-down inputs to the lower visual areas.
source: However, the strength of Hierarchical Frequency Tagging is in its ability to simultaneously tag both bottom-up and top-down inputs to the lower visual areas.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The IM signals, in the HFT paradigm, would reflect the crux of the hypothesis-testing function, namely, the comparison of prediction and sensory-driven signals, or the integration between state-units and error-units.
source: The IM signals, in our paradigm, would then reflect the crux of the hypothesis-testing function, namely, the comparison of prediction and sensory-driven signals, or the integration between state-units and error-units.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IM findings in the context of predictive coding.

claim: The certainty manipulation used in this study differs from several other studies whereby expectation is explicitly manipulated with a preceding cue.
source: An additional point worth noting is that the certainty manipulation we used in this study differs from several other studies (e.g. [Kok et al., 2013; Kok et al., 2012a]) whereby expectation is explicitly manipulated with a preceding cue.
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies supported by citations.

claim: In each trial certainty levels were learnt 'online' based on the proportion of images that appeared in that trial.
source: In each of the current study's trials certainty levels were learnt 'online' based on the proportion of images that appeared in that trial.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Operationalizing certainty through implicit learning may add sources of variability not controlled for, such as individual differences in learning rates.
source: Operationalizing certainty in this manner may add sources of variability we did not control for, such as individual differences in learning rates.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study design.

claim: Belief about the probability of an event is often shaped through repeated exposure to the same type of event, placing greater ecological validity to the study design.
source: On the other hand, belief about the probability of an event is often shaped through repeated exposure to the same type of event, placing greater ecological validity to our study design.
evidence: This is a justification for the study design.

claim: The evidence demonstrates the ability of the novel HFT technique to obtain a direct physiological measure of the integration of information derived from different levels of the cortical hierarchy during perception.
source: Overall, the evidence we have presented plausibly demonstrates the ability of the novel HFT technique to obtain a direct physiological measure of the integration of information derived from different levels of the cortical hierarchy during perception.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The results suggest that top-down, semantically tagged signals are integrated with bottom-up sensory-driven signals, and this integration is modulated by the level of certainty about the causes of the perceived input.
source: Supporting the predictive coding account of perception, our results suggest that top-down, semantically tagged signals are integrated with bottom-up sensory-driven signals, and this integration is modulated by the level of certainty about the causes of the perceived input.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: In SSVEP studies, the intensity (luminance or contrast) of a stimulus is typically modulated over time at a given frequency.
source: In steady-state-visual-evoked-potentials (SSVEP) studies, the intensity (luminance or contrast) of a stimulus is typically modulated over time at a given frequency, F Hz (i.e. the 'tagging frequency').
evidence: This is a description of the SSVEP method.

claim: Peaks at the tagging-frequency in the spectrum of the recorded signal are understood to reflect stimulus-driven neural activity.
source: Peaks at the tagging-frequency, f Hz, in the spectrum of the recorded signal are thus understood to reflect stimulus-driven neural activity.
evidence: This is a description of how SSVEP is interpreted.

claim: When the contrast or luminance of a stimulus is modulated over time, then all levels of the visual hierarchy are entrained at the tagging frequency.
source: When the contrast or luminance of a stimulus is modulated over time, then all levels of the visual hierarchy are entrained at the tagging frequency.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of SSVEP.

claim: It becomes difficult to dissociate frequency tagging related to low-level feature processing from that related to high-level semantic representations when using SSVEP.
source: Thus, it becomes difficult to dissociate frequency tagging related to low-level feature processing from that related to high-level semantic representations.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation of SSVEP.

claim: SWIFT overcomes the SSVEP limitation by scrambling image sequences in a way that maintains low-level physical features while modulating mid to high-level image properties.
source: Semantic wavelet-induced frequency-tagging (SWIFT) overcomes this obstacle by scrambling image sequences in a way that maintains low-level physical features while modulating mid to high-level image properties.
evidence: This is a description of the SWIFT method.

claim: SWIFT has been shown to constantly activate early visual areas while selectively tagging high-level object representations both in EEG and fMRI.
source: In this manner, SWIFT has been shown to constantly activate early visual areas while selectively tagging high-level object representations both in EEG (Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013) and fMRI (Koenig-Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013 and Koenig-Robert et al., 2015.

claim: SWIFT sequences were created by cyclic wavelet scrambling in the wavelets 3D space, allowing to scramble contours while conserving local low-level attributes such as luminance, contrast and spatial frequency.
source: In brief, sequences were created by cyclic wavelet scrambling in the wavelets 3D space, allowing to scramble contours while conserving local low-level attributes such as luminance, contrast and spatial frequency.
evidence: This is a description of the SWIFT method.

claim: The original unscrambled image appeared once in each cycle (1.3 Hz).
source: By construction, the original unscrambled image appeared once in each cycle (1.3 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the SWIFT method.

claim: A total of 27 participants were tested for this study.
source: A total of 27 participants were tested for this study (12 females; mean age = 28.9 y, std = 6.6).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Participants gave their written consent to participate in the experiment.
source: Participants gave their written consent to participate in the experiment.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures.

claim: Typical sample sizes in SSVEP and SWIFT studies range between 8–22 participants per experimental group.
source: Typical sample sizes in SSVEP and SWIFT studies range between 8–22 participants per experimental group (Chicherov and Herzog, 2015; Katyal et al., 2016; Koenig-Robert and VanRullen, 2013; Koenig-Robert et al., 2015; Painter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Experimental procedures were approved by the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee.
source: Experimental procedures were approved by the Monash University Human Research Ethics Committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: Participants were comfortably seated with their head supported by a chin rest 50 cm from the screen in a dimly lit room.
source: Participants were comfortably seated with their head supported by a chin rest 50 cm from the screen (CRT, 120 HZ refresh rate) in a dimly lit room.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: A total of 56 trials of 50 s each were presented to each participant.
source: A total of 56 such 50 s trials were presented to each participant.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Continuous EEG was acquired from 64 scalp electrodes using a Brain Products BrainAmp DC system.
source: Continuous EEG was acquired from 64 scalp electrodes using a Brain Products BrainAmp DC system.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition method.

claim: Data were sampled at 1000 Hz for 23 participants and at 500 Hz for the remaining four participants.
source: Data were sampled at 1000 Hz for 23 participants and at 500 Hz for the remaining four participants.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Data processing was performed using the EEGLAB toolbox in MATLAB.
source: Data processing was performed using the EEGLAB toolbox (Delorme and Makeig, 2004) in MATLAB.
evidence: This describes the data analysis tools used, supported by a citation.

claim: All data sampled at 1000 Hz were resampled to 500 Hz.
source: All data sampled at 1000 Hz were resampled to 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes a data preprocessing step.

claim: A high-pass filter was applied at 0.6 Hz.
source: A high-pass filter was applied at 0.6 Hz and data was converted to average reference.
evidence: This describes a data preprocessing step.

claim: Five participants whose correlation value r was lower than 0.9 were excluded from the analysis.
source: We excluded five participants whose correlation value r was lower than 0.9 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion and is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Five additional participants were excluded on the basis of poor EEG recording quality.
source: Five additional participants were excluded on the basis of this criterion for poor EEG recording (on average, 37% of cycles were noisy for these participants).
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion.

claim: A total of 17 remaining participants were included in the analysis.
source: A total of 17 remaining participants were included in the analysis.
evidence: This describes the final sample size.

claim: 5.5% of the trials were excluded based on within-participant accuracy criteria.
source: From this criterion, we excluded 5.5% of the trials (52 out of 952 trials in total, 0–5 trials out of 56 for any individual participant).
evidence: This describes trial exclusion.

claim: EEG signal amplitude was extracted at the tagging and intermodulation frequencies by applying the fast Fourier transform (FFT) over each trial.
source: EEG signal amplitude was extracted at the tagging and intermodulation frequencies by applying the fast Fourier transform (FFT) over each trial (50 s, 25,000 sample-points, frequency resolution = 0.02 Hz).
evidence: This describes the spectral analysis method.

claim: Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) at frequency f was computed by dividing the amplitude at f by the mean amplitude across 20 neighbouring frequencies.
source: Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) at frequency f was computed by dividing the amplitude at f by the mean amplitude across 20 neighbouring frequencies (from f-0.2Hz to f-0.02Hz and from f + 0.02 Hz to f + 0.2 Hz) (Srinivasan et al., 1999; Tononi and Edelman, 1998).
evidence: This describes the SNR calculation method, supported by citations.

claim: The analysis focused on the four lowest-order IM components.
source: While a large number of potential IM components exist in our data, we focused our analysis on the four lowest-order components (f1−2f2 = 7.4 Hz, f1−f2 = 8.7 Hz, f1+f2 = 11.3 Hz and f1+2f2 = 12.6 Hz, where f1 = 10 Hz and f2 = 1.3 Hz).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach.

claim: RStudio and lme4 were used to perform linear mixed-effect analysis of the data.
source: For analysis of the modulatory effects of certainty we used RStudio (RStudio Team, 2015) and lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) to perform linear mixed-effect analysis of the data.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis tools used, supported by citations.

claim: log2(amplitude SNR) was used as the dependant variable for all analyses.
source: We used log2(amplitude SNR) as the dependant variable for all analyses.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The amplitude SNR has a lower bound of 0 and does not distribute normally.
source: We chose this transformation because the amplitude SNR has a lower bound of 0 and does not distribute normally.
evidence: This is a justification for the statistical transformation used.

claim: The distribution of log2(SNR) is closer to a normal distribution and allows for better homoscedasticity in the linear models.
source: The distribution of log2(SNR) on the other hand is closer to a normal distribution and allows for better homoscedasticity in the linear models.
evidence: This is a justification for the statistical transformation used.

claim: Trials were divided into 10 certainty bins ranging from 1 (lowest certainty) to 10 (highest certainty).
source: In order to examine the modulatory effect of certainty, we divided trials into 10 certainty bins ranging from 1 (lowest certainty) to 10 (highest certainty).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach for examining certainty effects.

claim: Bin limits were defined in terms of the percentage of cycles at which the more frequent image appeared, thus creating 5%-wide bins.
source: Bin limits were defined in terms of the percentage of cycles at which the more frequent image appeared, thus creating 5%-wide bins (trials in which the more frequent image appeared in 50–55%, 55–60%, … and 95–100% of cycles are defined as bin 1, 2, ... and 10, respectively).
evidence: This describes how certainty bins were defined.

claim: All analyses were performed on a posterior ROI including 30 electrodes.
source: All analyses were performed on a posterior ROI (30 electrodes) including all centro-parietal (CPz and CP1-CP6), temporo-parietal (TP7-TP10), parietal (Pz and P1-P8), parieto-occipital (POz, PO3-PO4, and PO7-PO10) and occipital (Oz,O1 and O2) electrodes.
evidence: This describes the region of interest for the analysis.

claim: Likelihood ratio tests were performed to test for the significance of a given factor or interaction.
source: To test for the significance of a given factor or interaction, we performed likelihood ratio tests between the full model, as described above, and the reduced model which did not include the factor or interaction in question (Bates et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the statistical testing approach, supported by a citation.

claim: P values were adjusted using the false discovery rate when applicable.
source: When applicable, we adjusted p values using the false discovery rate (Yekutieli and Benjamini, 1999).
evidence: This describes the multiple comparison correction method, supported by a citation.
